name: David Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm David Olsen, forty-three, and I'm a junior miner driving a water truck at the big open pit. I wet down the haul roads, check the tank fittings, and radio when dust hides a bend. I came into this job from warehouse work, so I still ask the experienced operators where the road edge gives way after rain. My partner cleans rooms at a lodge, and our two children are in school; the mortgage and less than a month's savings keep me watching every shift on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my workmates AI hype doesn't change the dust on the haul road or my morning vehicle checks. I'd say the small reporting tools might save a few minutes, if someone checks their figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my water truck shifts to continue, though cancelled shifts would still put the mortgage under pressure. My partner's lodge hours change with bookings, so a quiet month can already empty our buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the water truck and logging road conditions each shift. I'd check the mine's digital report against my paper notes before sending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly steady about the technology, but money isn't easy in our house. Last winter a quiet week at the lodge made us wait to replace the washing machine belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the report tool now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The foreman showed me where the form fills in time and location. I check it against the notebook in my cab because I once entered the wrong road number and had to correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an ordinary month difficult?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two missed mine shifts and fewer lodge bookings would do it. We pay the mortgage first and shuffle everything else, so I wouldn't call our finances safe.

Check the mine's **digital report** against my paper notes before sending it.
feel: **Steady** about small technology changes at the mine.
**Worried** about bills when lodge hours or mine shifts fall.

fieldNote: Even an AI plateau leaves **household income** exposed to mine rosters and the partner's changing lodge hours.
He already checks a **digital form** against cab notes, showing limited but practical comfort with familiar software.

steps.text: Keep driving water truck shifts and checking digital reports against cab notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew dispatch software may change orders before robot vehicles take over the roads. I'd ask what happens to junior shifts if the office can route trucks with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my driving work lasts longer than the booking and planning jobs at the mine. I still worry a leaner roster could mean less pay before any robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the foreman to show me the trial route planner after a shift. I'd keep taking water truck shifts while checking whether mine maintenance openings are posted. I'd cancel our streaming subscription if two shifts disappear in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about a route planner if it actually keeps trucks apart on blind corners. I'm also nervous about someone using the same planner as an excuse to trim hours; the bills don't care why a shift vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try on the planner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare its route with the muddy bend near the crusher after rain. If it sends me there with a full tank, I'd tell the foreman why the route needs changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at maintenance openings already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The few mines around here don't advertise many driving jobs. An assistant role on this site would at least let me keep earning without moving the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI in 2028 could replace office planning first, while our hands-on driving has until about 2031. I'd ask the mine for a truck timetable and a place to train before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-five in 2028, I could still drive the water truck while software handles my route and reports. At forty-eight in 2031, robot trucks could take that wage, and the lodge cannot carry our mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the water truck while applying for workshop helper vacancies this year. I'd ask about paid mechanical training if the mine offers it before robot vehicles arrive. I'd stop buying new phones on monthly plans and put that payment toward emergency cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be frightened, but I would still have a couple of useful years behind the wheel. I need to spend those years getting into a workshop, not telling myself that dust keeps a person employed forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you offer a workshop today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can spot leaking fittings and explain where the pump lost pressure, but I can't claim to be a mechanic. I'd apply for helper work and learn from someone qualified if the mine would pay for training time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the robot date is 2031 in this picture, not next week. We'd drop phone upgrades and keep the children in their school while I looked for paid work on site.

I'd ask the mine for a **truck timetable** and a place to train before the robots arrive.
think: At forty-five in **2028**, I could still drive the water truck while software handles my route and reports.

feel: **Determined** to seek workshop work while driving income continues.
S2.quote: I'd apply for helper work and learn from someone qualified if the mine would pay for training time.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 planning automation** from 2031 robot driving and expects his own wage at risk then.
His **workshop application** is immediate, while training depends on a funded place and paid time away from truck shifts.

steps.text: Apply for workshop helper vacancies at the mine this year

Keep taking water truck shifts while applying for workshop work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 AGI gives the mine five years to show drivers a real replacement plan. I'd tell my neighbours robot trucks around 2034 could still push me out at fifty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have workshop experience by forty-eight if a helper vacancy opens before 2031. Without that move, I think the water truck wage is in danger when robots reach the pit in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for workshop helper roles as soon as one is advertised. I'd take a vehicle maintenance course if the mine pays the fees and allows shift release. I'd keep driving water runs while putting overtime into a repair fund for our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me less frantic than two, because I can collect experience rather than one rushed certificate. I still feel exposed: the house needs repairs and no one has offered me a workshop place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair are you saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roof above the back bedroom leaked during the last storm. I'd put overtime aside for that repair, since a wet room could eat whatever training money we scrape together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the helper applications fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the foreman what entry test I missed and try again when another opening comes. I might have to look outside mining, but I wouldn't move the whole family on a guess.

fieldNote: The five-year warning makes **workshop experience** possible, but his path depends on an actual opening and paid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell drivers ten years is enough time to ask for proper training, not a reason to ignore robot haulage. I'd say the mine owes us clear dates for equipment changes before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three in 2036, my children will be grown, but the mortgage may still need my wage. At fifty-six in 2039, robot trucks could remove the driving job; I cannot count on an unknown pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking water truck shifts and review the mine's equipment plan each year. I'd apply for workshop helper roles when vacancies appear rather than waiting until 2039. I'd take funded maintenance classes if the mine opens places that fit my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture this as a long turn in the road rather than a cliff. The time helps, though I'd still need a wage at fifty-six and would rather test workshop work before the truck is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in the family budget over a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children should be adults by then, so school costs will be different. We won't know whether they can support themselves, and I'm not putting their future wages into our mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the equipment plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want dates for the first robot water trucks and a list of jobs people can apply for. A poster promising opportunity won't tell me whether I can still pay the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I get only a few years of driving pay before robot trucks could arrive in 2031. I'd need the mine to publish its vehicle dates, offer paid workshop training, and let junior drivers apply for helper work early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how many training places there would be. If there are five spots for fifty drivers, I need to know that before I tell my partner we have a way through.

headlineQuote: I'd want dates for the first robot water trucks and a list of jobs people can apply for.
portrait: David is a **junior water truck** operator at a large mine, learning pit roads and vehicle checks.
A mortgage, two school-age children and less than a month's **savings** leave little room for lost shifts.
He tries **proven tools** against real road conditions and asks supervisors about practical failures.
He would apply for **workshop work** before robot vehicles arrive, if openings and paid training become available.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him only until about 2031 before robot trucks could displace his driving wage.
whatWouldHelp: Published **vehicle dates**, early helper applications and paid workshop training would let him plan around real openings.
He needs the **number of places** made clear before treating training as a secure route.
